items.title: Step 1
items.description:
Camperbot has created a coding journey blog page, but it looks like the page has some accessibility issues and bad practices. Your job in this workshop, is to fix these issues for Camperbot. The first set of errors has to deal with the use of headings. In a prior lesson, you learned that it is best practice to only use one `h1` per page. But it looks like Camperbot is a using a few `h1`s. Leave the `

Welcome to Camperbot's Blog

` alone and change the other `h1` elements to `h2` elements.

hints.text:
You should not alter the `

Welcome to Camperbot's Blog

`.
hints.test:
const heading = document.querySelectorAll("h1")[0];
assert.equal(heading?.textContent, "Welcome to Camperbot's Blog");

hints.text: You should change the `h1` element with the text of `My Journey Learning to Code` to an `h2` element.
You should change the `h1` element with the text of `Accessibility Matters` to an `h2` element.
You should change the `h1` element with the text of `What's Next?` to an `h2` element.

items.title: Step 2
items.description:
It looks like there are still some issues with the use of headings on the page. If you look at the first `div` element, there are two `h4` elements used as subheadings. A better practice would be to use `h3` elements for these subheadings since they are a level below the `h2` element.

Change the two `h4` elements to `h3` elements.

hints.text: Your `h4` element with the text of `Early Challenges` should be an `h3` element.
Your `h4` element with the text of `Breakthroughs` should be an `h3` element.

items.title: Step 3
items.description:

Change the `h5` element to an `h3` element.

hints.text: You should change the `h5` element to an `h3` element.

items.title: Step 4
items.description:
Below the main title of the page, there is a navigation section that contains links to each blog post. 

This section should be wrapped in a `nav` element to indicate its purpose as a navigation landmark.

hints.text: Your page should have a `nav` element.
hints.test:
const navElement = document.querySelector("nav");
assert.isNotNull(navElement);

hints.text:
Your `

Navigation

` should be inside the `nav` element.
Your `ul` element should be inside the `nav` element.
hints.test:
const ulElement = document.querySelector("nav ul");
assert.isNotNull(ulElement);

hints.text: Your `li` elements should be inside the `ul` element.
hints.test:
const liElements = document.querySelectorAll("nav ul li");
assert.isAtLeast(liElements.length, 3);

hints.text: You should not add any additional `ul`, `li` or `h2` elements.

items.title: Step 5
items.description:
In the blog page, there are a total of three blog posts wrapped inside generic `div` elements. But it would be better to use semantic elements to wrap each post. 

Change each `div` element that wraps each blog post to an `article` element.

hints.text: Your first `div` element for the first post should be changed to an `article` element.
hints.test:
const firstPost = document.querySelector("nav + article");
assert.isNotNull(firstPost);

hints.text: Your second `div` element for the second post should be changed to an `article` element.
hints.test:
const secondPost = document.querySelector("article + article");
assert.isNotNull(secondPost);

hints.text: Your third `div` element for the third post should be changed to an `article` element.
hints.test:
const thirdPost = document.querySelector("article + article + article");
assert.isNotNull(thirdPost);

items.title: Step 6
items.description: Since the entire section containing the blog posts represents the main content of the page, it should be wrapped in a `main` element. This helps screen readers and other assistive technologies understand the structure of the page better.

hints.text: You should have a `main` element.
hints.test:
const mainElement = document.querySelector("main");
assert.isNotNull(mainElement);

hints.text: Your `main` element should contain all three `article` elements.
hints.test:
const articles = document.querySelectorAll("main article");
assert.lengthOf(articles, 3);

items.title: Step 7
items.description:
For the last part of the workshop, there are a few changes needed for the contact section at the bottom.

The first change would be to wrap the contact section inside of a `footer` element. This will help screen readers identify this section as the footer of the page.

hints.text: Your page should have a `footer` element.
hints.test:
const footerElement = document.querySelector("footer");
assert.isNotNull(footerElement);

hints.text: Your `footer` element should contain an `h3` element with the text `Contact Me`.
Your `footer` element should contain a `p` element with the text `Email me at camperbot@blog.io`.

items.description:

items.title: Step 9
items.description:
The last change will be to the email text inside of the footer. In earlier lessons and workshops, you learned how to work with the `mailto` link like this: ```html

Email me at janedoe@email.com

``` Start by wrapping the `camperbot@blog.io` email address inside of an anchor element. Then, add the `href` attribute to the anchor element and set it equal to `mailto:camperbot@blog.io`. With that last change, you have successfully resolved all of the issues in the blog page!

hints.text: Your `camperbot@blog.io` email address should be wrapped inside of an anchor element.
Your anchor element should have an `href` attribute with a value of `mailto:camperbot@blog.io`.
hints.test:
const anchor = document.querySelector("footer a");
assert.strictEqual(anchor?.getAttribute("href"), "mailto:camperbot@blog.io");
